_comment: The caller-param NAMES that make a capability handler owe a decision, and what
each one becomes on the host. This is the sole input to BOTH classification
scans — the Go one over cmd/brain's dispatch switch, the regex one over the
desktop's hubCapabilities.ts — and until this file existed it was pinned by
nothing at all.
That is not a hypothetical. Deleting nine names from capspec.go's
dangerousParams map (configDir, mcpItemIds, command, binaries, extraArgs,
filename, data, bytesB64, url) left the entire Go suite green; adding
configDir + command + mcpItemIds to terminals.create afterwards — the original
unclassified-process-identifier defect, three times over — was green too. The
map lives in a non-test file, so the disarm does not even read as a test edit in
review. A detector whose input can be emptied without a failure is a comment.
TWO blocks, because the detector has two halves:
`params` — name -> kind, the DENYLIST. A name here forces a decision wherever
a handler binds it: it is the method's PathParam field (the bus
confines it), or the method's per-param ParamDecision says what it
is and why it is safe. Kinds: path, filename, executable, argv,
shell, env, url, port, id, regex, permission, inert.
`stems`  — the SHAPE heuristic, which exists because a denylist of names is
only as good as the namer's imagination: `entrypoint`, `exe`,
`launcher` and `shellPath` are all argv[0] on terminals.create and
not one of them is spelled `shell` or `command`. A param name whose
tokens (camelCase / snake_case / dotted) include a stem, and which
`params` does not know, fails the scans with an instruction: add it
to the vocabulary, or record it in `inertExceptions` with the
reason its shape is a coincidence.
`inertExceptions` — that escape hatch, name -> reason. Empty today: every
stem-shaped name either provider binds is already in `params`. An
entry here is a claim a reviewer should read, which is the point of
keeping it in the corpus rather than in a map nobody diffs.
Owner: services/hub/internal/capspec/capspec.go (dangerousParams, paramStems,
knownInertParams). The names come from BOTH provider trees — `bytesB64` exists
only in the Go brain, `contents` only in the desktop — but both SCANS are Go, so
this golden lives here rather than in contracts/. contracts/ is for fixtures two
LANGUAGES load (cmd/brain/contracts_test.go fails any fixture with fewer than two,
in two languages), and a TS loader written only to satisfy that count would be the
dead contract that guard exists to prevent. What matters for review is the same:
the vocabulary is a diffable file, and shrinking it fails a named test.
Shrinking this file is allowed and sometimes right. Doing it SILENTLY is not:
the golden and the map are held equal in both directions by
TestDangerousParamVocabularyMatchesTheGolden.
